title: Memory: Retrieval, Forgetting, Ebbinghaus, Mnemonics
summary: Retrieval failure; inhibition; motivated forgetting; Hermann Ebbinghaus; decay theory; two-factor model (Bjork); mnemonics; flashbulb memories; synaptic theory; long-term potentiation.
objectives: Explain LTP as neural basis of memory.
revision: Retrieval failure = stored but inaccessible. Forgetting = decay (time) or interference (competition). Ebbinghaus curve = rapid initial drop, then plateau. LTP = synaptic strengthening = neural memory basis. Mnemonics = memory aids.
traps: Forgetting curve = rapid initial forgetting, then levels off.
LTP = neural basis of memory (synaptic strengthening).
confusions: Believing flashbulb memories are always accurate.

notes.t: Retrieval failure occurs when information is stored in memory but cannot be accessed due to missing retrieval cues.
Hermann Ebbinghaus pioneered the scientific study of memory and forgetting using nonsense syllables. The forgetting curve shows rapid initial forgetting that levels off.
Decay theory proposes that memory traces weaken over time if not used.
Bjork's two-factor model proposes that forgetting depends on both storage strength and retrieval strength.
Mnemonics are memory aids (acronyms, acrostics, method of loci, chunking) that improve encoding and retrieval.
Flashbulb memories are vivid, detailed memories of emotionally significant events (e.g., where you were when hearing major news).
LTP is the strengthening of synaptic connections based on recent patterns of activity, considered a neural basis for learning and memory.
UGC NET frequently asks about Ebbinghaus's forgetting curve, decay vs interference, and LTP as neural basis of memory.

mnemonics.text: D — Decay (traces fade), I — Interference (competing memories), M — Motivated (repression)
